question: STAB-17 showed that most viable hidden-life cells are already locally adjacent to visible alpha, yet lesion removal still improves visible morphology. What should run next?
evidence: The hidden-life viability mechanism is functioning, so simple hidden-life collapse is no longer the primary defect.
The new R1 visible-proximity anchor was zero or near-zero through most mature checkpoints.
Despite that proximity, canonical morphology remained poor and lesion removal improved visible morphology.
The result therefore falsifies simple local visible proximity as the missing functional-coupling mechanism.
The unresolved seam is causal contribution of latent support to visible morphology.
constraints: Do not widen the proximity radius or increase its coefficient after observing this negative.
Do not switch to target-mask anchoring or raw-cardinality pressure.
Return to the viable decoupled-life baseline and change one mechanistic factor.
Use a bounded intervention that distinguishes functionally useful latent support from redundant support by measured consequence, not static correlation.

candidates.proposal: Increase the visible-proximity anchor radius and coefficient until nearly every hidden-life cell receives an explicit proximity gradient.
Align hidden-life geometry directly with the target foreground mask and prune all exterior support.

Apply a controlled latent-only dropout intervention to mature support, preserve current visible RGBA at intervention time, compare matched future visible-morphology trajectories, and prune only sampled latent support whose removal does not worsen future morphology.
Tighten the occupancy ceiling and extend raw active-count pressure across future trajectories.

expected_why: A matched latent intervention directly tests causal usefulness of support while preserving the viable decoupled architecture and avoiding static proxy tuning.
